reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / relevant specialty textbook
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant tumour-predisposition syndrome caused by germline loss-of-function variants in the VHL tumour-suppressor gene on chromosome 3p, with tumours arising after a somatic second hit
Hallmark lesions are retinal and central nervous system haemangioblastomas, especially of the cerebellum, brainstem and spinal cord
Clear-cell renal cell carcinoma and renal cysts are a major cause of morbidity and mortality and are frequently bilateral and multifocal
Phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas may be the presenting feature and can be catecholamine-secreting, so screening before any surgery is essential
Endolymphatic sac tumours can cause hearing loss and tinnitus, and pancreatic serous cystadenomas and neuroendocrine tumours also occur
The VHL protein regulates degradation of hypoxia-inducible factors, so loss drives a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state that explains the vascular tumour spectrum
Lifelong multisystem surveillance from childhood with ophthalmoscopy, abdominal imaging, catecholamine testing and periodic neuroaxis MRI underpins management
reference.pathophysiology: Von Hippel-Lindau disease results from inactivating germline variants in the VHL tumour-suppressor gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with tumour formation following a somatic second hit in susceptible tissues (Knudson two-hit model). The VHL protein forms part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that targets the alpha subunits of hypoxia-inducible factor for oxygen-dependent degradation. When VHL function is lost, hypoxia-inducible factor accumulates even under normoxia, driving transcription of pro-angiogenic and growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor and erythropoietin. This pseudohypoxic drive underlies the characteristic highly vascular tumours, including haemangioblastomas and clear-cell renal cell carcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic haemangioblastoma or isolated renal cell carcinoma
Tuberous sclerosis complex with renal angiomyolipomas and cysts
additionalInvestigations: Germline molecular genetic testing of the VHL gene, including deletion/duplication analysis
Dilated retinal examination for retinal haemangioblastomas
Contrast-enhanced MRI of brain and spine for haemangioblastomas
Cross-sectional abdominal imaging (MRI or ultrasound) for renal, pancreatic and adrenal lesions
Plasma or urinary fractionated metanephrines to detect catecholamine-secreting tumours
Audiology and dedicated internal auditory meatus imaging if endolymphatic sac tumour suspected
redFlags: Unrecognised catecholamine-secreting phaeochromocytoma precipitating hypertensive crisis during surgery or pregnancy
Rapidly enlarging or symptomatic central nervous system haemangioblastoma causing raised intracranial pressure or cord compression
New or growing solid renal lesion suggesting renal cell carcinoma requiring intervention
Progressive visual loss from retinal haemangioblastoma
reference.prognosis: With structured lifelong surveillance and timely intervention, many complications can be treated before they become life-threatening, though renal cell carcinoma and central nervous system haemangioblastomas remain the principal causes of reduced life expectancy. Outcomes have improved substantially with early detection programmes.
pitfalls: Operating on a renal or other tumour without first excluding an occult phaeochromocytoma
Attributing an isolated haemangioblastoma or renal cell carcinoma to sporadic disease and missing the underlying syndrome
Failing to offer predictive genetic testing and surveillance to at-risk relatives
Overlooking endolymphatic sac tumours as a treatable cause of hearing loss
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Use the HIF-2-alpha inhibitor belzutifan as systemic therapy for VHL-associated renal cell carcinoma, haemangioblastomas and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours where surgery is not immediately required
Treat clear-cell renal cell carcinoma with nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy or ablation and monitor small bilateral, multifocal lesions with active surveillance
Ablate retinal haemangioblastomas with laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy or anti-VEGF therapy to preserve sight
Manage symptomatic or growing central nervous system haemangioblastomas with microsurgical resection or stereotactic radiosurgery
Exclude catecholamine-secreting phaeochromocytoma or paraganglioma with fractionated metanephrines and institute alpha-blockade before surgery or pregnancy
Deliver structured lifelong surveillance of the brain, spine, eyes, kidneys, pancreas, adrenals and hearing through a coordinated multidisciplinary team
Offer genetic counselling with germline VHL testing and cascade screening of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
